verifier.name: Step 9 -- the verifier had to be fixed before 7 GB could go through it
verifier.finding: forge_verify re-parsed every staged file with PyKotor, and for a texture that meant read_tpc decoding every mipmap into memory. Fine on a handful of files. On step 9's 1,033 textures totalling 7.1 GB it walked the worker from 366 MB to 3.1 GB of working set, climbing about 550 MB a minute with no plateau and roughly 60 percent of the batch still to go. The run was killed rather than gambled on -- nothing had been deployed, staging was intact, and stopping cost only a re-run.
verifier.fix: Decoding pixels was never the point. The question a verify gate answers is whether the engine will choke on a file, and for a texture the 128-byte header settles it: plausible dimensions, a known encoding byte, and enough bytes present for the first mipmap. O(1) memory. 969 textures now check in 0.2 seconds against 10-plus minutes unfinished, and it still refuses a file truncated to a third, a 60-byte stub, and a corrupted encoding byte -- each with a diagnostic naming what is wrong.
verifier.models: MDL and MDX had been passing through unchecked, so they got a header check too, and it took two corrections to get right. The first read rawDataSize as part of the MDL and declared every healthy model in the game corrupt -- it is actually the size of the PAIRED .mdx. The second called an oversized .mdx corruption, until stock dor_mal02 turned out to declare 12,888 bytes against an .mdx holding 12,896: BioWare ships 8 bytes of padding, and the game has always loaded it. So the pair check is asymmetric now -- a short .mdx is fatal, a long one is padding. Vanilla is the oracle.
verifier.bonus: The model check then confirmed the saber finding a second and independent way. w_lghtsbr_001.mdl declares a zero-length vertex buffer and its .mdx is zero bytes: 'paired .mdx empty as declared'. The first proof came from matching node-name strings; this one comes from the model's own header. All 362 models in override/ pass.

sabers.name: Step 7 -- 31 zero-byte model files, and why they are correct
sabers.finding: Lightsaber Hilt Variety ships 62 .mdx vertex-buffer files and 31 of them are ZERO BYTES -- in the author's original zip, not as an extraction artifact, and the zip passes its CRC. Worse, the game's own copies of those same ResRefs carry 10,848 bytes each. Read naively that is a mod blanking every lightsaber in the game, and the first automated verdict said exactly that: DO NOT DEPLOY. It was wrong, and the reason is worth keeping. The 31 empty ones are all named w_dblsbr_NNN / w_lghtsbr_NNN / w_shortsbr_NNN -- weapon models. Alongside them ship 31 NEW models named dblsbr_blue, lghtsbr_gold, shortsbr_turq and so on, each carrying 10,688 bytes of real geometry. Opening w_dblsbr_001.mdl shows it grew from 57,392 to 80,650 bytes and gained three node names absent from stock: ref_hilt, dummy_blade, and dblsbr_blue. The weapon model was rewritten into a rig that REFERENCES a separate model holding the mesh. The vertex data moved; it was not deleted. That is the documented Aspyr hilt fix, and the empty .mdx is correct by construction.
sabers.heuristic_note: The first check also required the rewritten MDL to be larger than stock. Six models failed that and were flagged -- all six come back at exactly 42,065 bytes, one uniform rig template replacing six different stock hilts. Identical sizes across six distinct models is evidence of a systematic rebuild, not of damage. The size test was dropped; the two that mean something are whether the model carries the reference node and whether the model it names actually ships with real geometry. All 31 pass both.
sabers.downstream: w_dblsbr_001.mdl also references W_LSabreBlue01 -- the exact blade texture step 6 installs, which is the install order justifying itself. And the Ultimate High Resolution Texture Pack at step 9 ships w_Lghtsbr_001.tpc: a .tpc beats a .tga for the same ResRef, so letting it through would override this fix and bring the glitched hilts straight back. It has to be excluded.

tslrcm.name: TSLRCM 1.8.6 -- the Russian dialog.tlk you nearly got
tslrcm.finding: The installer is Inno Setup 5.6, which innoextract can open without running it -- so the entire 674-file payload was read before a single byte reached the game. That is how this surfaced: TWO dialog.tlk files ship inside, both writing to the same destination in the game root, and the language chosen at install time is what picks between them. One is English. One is Russian. Both carry 136,375 entries, so a wrong pick would not look like a failure -- it would look like a successful TSLRCM install with every line of dialogue in Russian. The install was therefore run with /LANG=english forced, and the result verified by hash rather than by eye.

step1.name: 3C-FD Tool v4.1.2
step1.finding: Not a GUI to click through. It is a 32-bit self-extracting PowerShell bundle: running it once unpacks a 3cfd\ folder holding patcher.ps1, a GUI script, and one declarative JSON per patch. patcher.ps1 takes -File, -Patch, -DryRun and -Backup, detects 'already applied' by searching for the replace pattern, refuses on a find/replace length mismatch, and never changes file length. So the step ran headless and dry-runnable, which is the forge's whole doctrine handed over for free. Never use its -ApplyAll: the patches folder holds K1, GOG and Borderless variants side by side.
